title.en: Aponibolinayen and Algaba: The Mango and the Reviving Perfumes
title.zh: 阿波妮波莉納衍與阿爾加巴：芒果與復魂香

region.en: Dagala (Tinguian mythic town), Abra Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿布拉省達加拉（丁桂安神話城鎮，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale, told by Magwati of Lagangilang; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (Magwati's version), pp. 42-47

summary.en: Dying for a taste of Algaba's mangoes, Aponibolinayen sends Dalonagan with an egg that hatches into a crowing rooster by the time they reach the snake-fenced town of Dagala; Algaba's weapons weep tears of oil and blood when he moves to strike — a sign they are kin. He uses his power so she will die as he arrives, then revives her with three whips of perfume, marries her when the betel-quids turn to rows of holeless agates, and is renamed Aponitolau when he goes home to Kadalayapan.
summary.zh: 阿波妮波莉納衍渴望阿爾加巴的芒果而病危；信使達洛納甘攜蛋上路，抵達蟒蛇護城的達加拉時雛雞已長成啼鳴雄雞。阿爾加巴欲戰，其兵刃卻滴油淚血淚——這是親族之兆。他運神力使她恰在抵家時死去，再以三道香霧喚她復生；檳榔渣化為成排無孔瑪瑙珠，二人成婚；回卡達拉雅潘後，他獲賜新名阿波尼托勞。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative told by Magwati, a man of Lagangilang, Abra; collected 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole; archival record. The weeping weapons are a kinship omen; perfumes are used as reviving magic, named not described operationally.

passages.text: 'I am anxious to eat the mango fruit which belongs to Algaba of Dagala,' said Aponibolinayen, and when she said this she was almost dying, and she repeated it. 'Does she not know that anyone who goes there cannot return?' asked Dalonagan; but Aponibalagen sent Dalonagan and Dina-ogan with a belt and earrings to trade for the fruit, and Dalonagan took an egg which he held all the time they walked — and when they had almost arrived in Dagala the chicken had become a rooster which could crow. At the spring the women told them to follow the sagang (head poles) to the house of Algaba, and when they passed the defensive fence, which was made of boa constrictors, the snakes did not notice them, for the snakes slept.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), Magwati's version of 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Algaba ran home very angry when he heard enemies had come inside the town, and went to get his headaxe and spear — but when he took them down the weapons shed tears which were of oil. 'What is the matter with my weapons that they weep oil? Perhaps these men are my relatives,' said the angry man; he dropped them, and when he took another set they shed bloody tears. The two men had come to buy the mango fruit for Aponibolinayen, who was nearly dead; Algaba showed them his yard where all the stones were gold, and smiled at the belt they offered: 'How pretty it is! I think the lady who owns this is much prettier.' He picked two mangoes himself and came along, saying to his alan mother, 'Do not feel anxious concerning me while I am gone... watch for enemies who come inside the town.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), Magwati's version of 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the way Algaba used his power so that the sick woman would feel very ill and nearly die; reaching the well that belonged to Aponibolinayen, he used his power so that she would die — and she truly died. But when he looked at her she was a lady without an equal for beauty, and he took the body in his arms: 'I use my power so that when I whip my perfume kaladakad she will move directly,' and the body moved; 'I use my power so that when I whip my perfume banawes she will say Wes,' and she at once said Wes; 'I use my power so that when I whip my perfume she will wake up,' and she woke up — 'Wes, how long my sleep was!' 'You have been dead,' said Algaba. Their rings exchanged themselves while he held her, and when she had regained her breath he divided the mango fruit and gave it to her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), Magwati's version of 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He made her chew betel-nut, for it is bad for them to talk when they do not know each other's names: 'My name is Algaba of Dagala. I have looked in all parts of the world for a wife, but I did not find anyone like you, and now I have found you, and I want you to be married to me.' 'My name is Aponibolinayen of Kaodanan, sister of Aponibalagen,' she said; and when they laid down their quids they were rows of agate beads which have no holes, so it was good for them to be married. They went to Dagala, where the alan mother gave them all her valuable things and flew away; at the Sayang they learned through the betel quids that Algaba was the brother of Aponigawani, and when all had been paid — the balaua filled nine times with jars — they took him to Kadalayapan, where he was renamed Aponitolau.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), Magwati's version of 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.

title.en: Asibowan of Gegawan and the Hidden Bride at the Spring of Lisnayan
title.zh: 格加萬的阿西博萬與莉斯納揚泉畔的隱藏新娘

region.en: Gegawan and Lisnayan springs (Tinguian mythic places), Abra Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿布拉省格加萬與莉斯納揚泉（丁桂安神話之地，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (Asibowan episodes), pp. 52-57

summary.en: A bird guides Aponitolau to Gegawan, where Asibowan cooks her fish-stick into a fish and lives alone; he stays nine months, siring Binaklingan, whose golden house his parents wake to find beside their own. Urged home by the pile of searchers' bones nine times the size of a balaua, Aponitolau later uses magic to draw all the sheltered girls to the spring of Lisnayan, where Aponibolinayen bathes like half a rainbow and vanishes into the betel-nut leaves. Found, she is carried off to Kadalayapan; her brother learns of the marriage when Langa-an, drunk on basi, lets it slip; Asibowan herself is compelled to attend the Sayang by the gold betel-nut that grows on her pig's head.
summary.zh: 飛鳥引路，阿波尼托勞至格加萬；阿西博萬以魚簽變魚、獨居一室。他留居九月，育女碧納克林安——其金屋一夜飛至祖屋旁。搜尋者的獸骨堆成九座巴勞瓦大小，他終被催歸。後他以神力使避光深閨的姑娘們燥熱出浴；莉斯納揚泉邊，阿波妮波莉納衍浴姿如半道彩虹，旋即隱入檳榔葉間。尋獲之後，她被接往卡達拉雅潘；兄長在朗嘉安酒後失言中方知婚事；阿西博萬亦被長在她豬頭上的金檳榔逼赴塞揚宴。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative recorded 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole; archival record. The lala-am ('those within') — sheltered girls who never go outdoors — are a Tinguian custom the storytellers explain as protecting the prettiest girls' skin; Kaboniyan is a powerful spirit to whom Asibowan claims kinship.

passages.text: 'Sinogyaman, come and oil my hair so that I can go to war,' said Aponitolau — and, telling his wives Sinogyaman and Sinagayan he was going to fight, he set out for Gegawan, where Asibowan lived, whom every one said was a pretty girl. A bird met him and showed him the way. At the ladder of her house Asibowan claimed her guest had lost his way to Nagsingkawan and invited him in, cooking for him; while they talked he saw her break the fish-stick and put it in the pot and watched it become a fish — and she confessed she had no husband, and told him her name: 'Asibowan of Gegawan, who lives alone in the field, who has no neighbors, for this is my fortune.' So Aponitolau stayed with her nine months, while his father and mother searched for him with many people, killing many animals to feed the searchers until all their animals were gone; the bones which they threw away made a pile nine times as large as the balaua.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (Asibowan episodes); not verbatim.

passages.text: Asibowan became pregnant and gave birth to a girl they called Binaklingan; when she bathed the baby it grew one span, for she used magical power, until the child could walk. Aponitolau saw the pile of bones the searchers had thrown away, nine times larger than the balaua, and said the best thing was to go home to Kadalayapan — but Asibowan said it was not good for them to be married, because she had less magical power than he: 'The best thing for you to do is to go home and find a woman whom you should marry, and then when you are married you make Sayang, and I will come to Kadalayapan.' She commanded that a house be made for Binaklingan, and it was all of gold, finished in the middle of the night — and she used magic so that the golden house went to Kadalayapan, where Aponitolau woke to many roosters crowing and many people talking, and Langa-an saw the different house beside their own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (Asibowan episodes); not verbatim.

passages.text: Five days after coming home, Aponitolau went at evening to the spring of Lisnayan, and used magic so that all the pretty girls who never go outdoors felt hot and went to the spring to bathe; Aponibolinayen felt very hot and went to bathe, and she looked like the half of a rainbow. 'Do not wound me in more than one place so I will not have so much to cure,' she said as he came; 'If I was an enemy I would have killed you at once,' said Aponitolau, cutting a betel-nut into two pieces, since it is bad to talk when they do not know each other's names. She told him her brother had put her at the place close to the spring of Lisnayan so that no one would see her, 'but you have found me' — and while they were talking she used magic so that she vanished and went among the betel-nuts on the branch of the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (Asibowan episodes); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the second night he went again, and when he looked up where there were many betel-nuts he saw Aponibolinayen taking a bath: 'Now I am going to take you home.' She feared her brother would hate her, but he took her to Kadalayapan and sent his mother to tell Aponibalagen. Langa-an crossed on her belt spread upon the water, and when the drops of water from her body became agate beads with no holes, the women dipping water said, 'How strange are the people of Kadalayapan.' Drinking basi with Aponibalagen and Ebang, who denied having any daughter, the old woman became drunk and let out that Aponibolinayen was in Kadalayapan — and Aponibalagen's heart jumped, for he had hidden his sister at Lisnayan so no one would see her. Langa-an paid the marriage price, the balaua filled nine times; and at the Sayang that followed, Asibowan herself was compelled to come by the oiled betel-nut covered with gold, which grew on her big pig's head until she promised; there Iwaginan danced with her while Gimbagonan, whose necklaces were of big jars that clattered so she could not hear the gansas, was jealous.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (Asibowan episodes); not verbatim.
